review.reason: Read the public abstract and supplementary test conditions, comparisons, heat-exchanger design, and economic assumptions. Main text is subscription-only; claims are confined to accessible primary evidence.

item.title: A 250-kilowatt system for co-production of hydrogen and fresh water from seawater
item.headline: Putting hydrogen production’s waste heat to work desalinating seawater
item.authors: Shang Jiang, Peixin Zhu, Yanting Liu, and Dehui Deng
item.summary: A 250-kW system coupled water electrolysis with seawater distillation. Its 40-day test used daily starts and stops with four hours at steady load, leaving long-term durability unresolved.

evidence.question: Can electrolyser waste heat supply desalination?
evidence.method: 20-kW and 250-kW systems, operating measurements, and separate economic modeling.
evidence.limitations: Pilot operation differs from the large plant assumed in cost calculations.

explainer.finding: The larger system produced hydrogen and surplus fresh water by using electrolysis waste heat to distil seawater.
explainer.method: The supplement reports 100 days of testing at 20 kW and 40 at 250 kW, each with daily four-hour steady-load periods. The larger system used electrolysis at 85°C and distillation around 44°C.
explainer.meaning: Like using an engine’s heat to warm a cabin, useful output comes from heat that otherwise needs removing. Here the recovered heat helps separate water from salt.
explainer.limits: Costs are modeled, including a 30-year plant life and initially 97% utilization. Those assumptions were not demonstrated by the short trials. This review uses the public abstract and supplement; the main text is paywalled.
